title: States of matter
summary: Learn the solid, liquid, gas and plasma states, changes of state and the phase diagram.
cards.0.h: Kinetic theory and the three states
cards.0.p: By kinetic theory, particles are always moving, and they speed up as the temperature rises. The state of a substance is set by a contest between the attraction among particles and their motion. In a solid, attraction wins. In a gas, motion wins.
cards.0.key: In a liquid, attraction and motion are balanced. Temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy.
cards.0.once.soru: What happens to water molecules when you heat the water in a container?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: Temperature is a measure of the particles' average energy of motion.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: The size of the molecules does not change. What changes is their speed and the distance between them.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: Particles never stop. They speed up when heated.
cards.1.p: In crystalline solids the particles form an ordered lattice, and the substance melts sharply at a definite temperature. Salt and ice are examples. In amorphous solids there is no order, and the substance softens slowly as it is heated. Glass and plastic are examples.
cards.1.key: Glass is an amorphous solid. It has no definite melting point and softens over a range of temperatures when heated.
cards.2.p: The force that holds a crystal together decides its properties. Ionic crystals (NaCl) are hard and brittle. Covalent network crystals (diamond) are very hard to melt. Molecular crystals (ice) melt easily. Metallic crystals (Cu) conduct.
cards.2.etk.soru: Match each solid with its type of crystal.
cards.2.key: When a molecular solid melts, the weak interactions between molecules break, not the covalent bonds.
cards.2.once.soru: Why does diamond melt only at a very high temperature?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.yazi: It is a covalent network crystal
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: A whole diamond is one covalent network. To melt it, strong bonds must break.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: Diamond is made only of carbon atoms and contains no ions.
cards.3.p: Liquids flow because their particles slide past each other. The resistance to flow is called viscosity. Liquids with strong attractions have high viscosity, which is why honey flows more slowly than water. Viscosity drops as a liquid warms up.
cards.3.key: If you heat a liquid, its viscosity drops. Warm honey flows more easily.
cards.4.p: A molecule at the surface is pulled only sideways and inward. So the surface behaves like a stretched skin, and this is called surface tension. Water has high surface tension because of hydrogen bonds. Soap and heat lower surface tension.
cards.4.key: Drops take a round shape, because surface tension makes the surface as small as possible.
cards.4.once.soru: How does a water strider walk on water without sinking?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: The water surface acts like a stretched skin and holds up the light insect.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: The insect does not sink into the water. The water surface holds it up.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: Viscosity is resistance to flow. It does not explain being held up at the surface.
cards.5.p: In a closed container, once the rates of evaporation and condensation are equal, the pressure of the vapor is called the equilibrium vapor pressure. Vapor pressure rises with temperature. Liquids with weak attractions between particles, such as acetone, have high vapor pressure.
cards.5.key: Vapor pressure does not depend on the amount of liquid. Liquids with high vapor pressure and low boiling points, such as acetone and ether, are called volatile.
cards.6.p: When the vapor pressure equals the outside pressure, bubbles form inside the liquid, and this is called boiling. Evaporation happens at any temperature and only at the surface. If the outside pressure drops, the boiling point drops too.
cards.6.key: On a mountain, water boils below 100 °C. In a pressure cooker it boils at about 120 °C, which is why food cooks quickly there.
cards.7.p: The ratio of the vapor pressure in the air to the saturated vapor pressure is called relative humidity. At 100% relative humidity the air is saturated. When humidity is high, sweat evaporates poorly and the air feels hotter.
cards.7.svg#6: High humidity, sweat evaporates poorly: the air feels hotter
cards.7.key: The temperature your body senses is called the feels-like temperature. Relative humidity is the vapor pressure divided by the saturated vapor pressure, times 100.
cards.7.once.soru: At the same 32 °C, why does a humid coastal city feel hotter than a dry desert city?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: The air is close to full of vapor. So sweat cannot evaporate and cool the body.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: The temperature is the same in both cities. The difference is the humidity.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: What makes the felt difference is sweating, which depends on humidity.
cards.8.p: In a very hot gas, or one in a strong electric field, atoms lose electrons. This ionized gas, made of electrons and positive ions, is called plasma. The Sun, lightning and neon lights are examples of plasma.
cards.8.key: Plasma conducts electricity and gives off light. Most of the visible matter in the universe is plasma, and stars are made of plasma.
cards.8.once.soru: Which one is in the plasma state?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: In lightning the air gets so hot that atoms lose electrons and an ionized gas forms.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: Water vapor is an ordinary gas, and its molecules are not ionized.
cards.9.p: A substance above its critical temperature cannot be liquefied even by compression, and it is called a gas. A substance below its critical temperature is called a vapor, and it liquefies under pressure. That is why propane can be kept as a liquid in a tank.
cards.9.key: At room temperature oxygen is a gas, and water vapor is a vapor. To liquefy a gas, you must first cool it below its critical temperature.
cards.9.once.soru: At room temperature, oxygen will not liquefy no matter how much you compress it. Why?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.yazi: It is above its critical temperature
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: Oxygen's critical temperature is about −119 °C. At room temperature, pressure alone is not enough.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: Size does not decide liquefaction. The temperature relative to the critical value does.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: Above the critical temperature, no amount of pressure causes liquefaction.
cards.10.h: Changes of state and the heating curve
cards.10.p: Melting, evaporation and sublimation absorb heat, so they are endothermic changes. Their reverses release heat, so they are exothermic changes. On the flat parts of the heating curve, the heat added goes into overcoming attraction, and the temperature stays constant.
cards.10.key: On the flat parts of the curve Q = m·L is used, and on the sloped parts Q = m·c·ΔT. A steam burn is worse than a boiling-water burn, because steam releases extra heat as it condenses.
cards.11.p: A phase diagram shows which state a substance is in at a given temperature and pressure. At the triple point solid, liquid and gas exist together. Water's triple point is 0.01 °C and 0.006 atm.
cards.11.etk.soru: Tap the numbers on water's phase diagram.
cards.11.etk.noktalar.0.acik: At low temperature and high pressure, water is ice.
cards.11.etk.noktalar.1.acik: Between the melting and vaporization curves, water is liquid.
cards.11.etk.noktalar.2.acik: At high temperature and low pressure, water is a gas (vapor).
cards.11.etk.noktalar.3.acik: At the triple point, solid, liquid and gas are in equilibrium together. For water this point is 0.01 °C and about 0.006 atm.
cards.11.etk.noktalar.4.acik: The liquid–gas curve ends here. Above this temperature, water vapor cannot be liquefied by pressure.
cards.11.key: On the curves, two states are in equilibrium. Water is an exception, because ice melts when pressure rises. CO₂'s triple point is at 5.1 atm, so dry ice sublimes at 1 atm.
cards.12.p:
• The state of a substance is set by the attraction between particles and their energy of motion.
• Crystalline solids melt sharply, and amorphous solids melt by softening.
• A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the outside pressure.
• Below the critical temperature there is vapor, above it gas. Plasma is ionized gas.
• For a change of state use Q = m·L, and for heating use Q = m·c·ΔT.
cards.12.svg#5: while the state changes, a pure substance's temperature stays constant
quiz.0.q: 20 g of ice at 0 °C melts and warms to water at 20 °C. How many calories of heat does it absorb in total? (Heat of fusion L = 80 cal/g, specific heat of water c = 1 cal/g·°C)
quiz.0.e: Melting (the flat part) takes Q = m·L = 20·80 = 1600 cal. Warming (the sloped part) takes Q = m·c·ΔT = 20·1·20 = 400 cal. The total is 2000 cal.
quiz.1.q: Water is boiled in an open pot at the places below. Order the boiling temperatures from lowest to highest.
quiz.1.e: Water boils when its vapor pressure equals the outside pressure. Higher up, air pressure drops and the boiling point falls. In a pressure cooker the pressure is above 1 atm.
quiz.2.q: Match each event with the fact that explains it.
quiz.2.ciftler.0.0: Dry ice turning into gas at 1 atm without melting
quiz.2.ciftler.1.0: Ice melting below 0 °C under high pressure
quiz.2.ciftler.1.1: Ice is less dense than water
quiz.2.ciftler.2.0: Propane staying liquid in a tank
quiz.2.ciftler.3.0: Pasta cooking slowly on a mountain
quiz.2.e: 1 atm is below CO₂'s triple point, so liquid CO₂ cannot form. Ice is less dense than water, so pressure makes melting easier. Propane is below its critical temperature, so it liquefies under pressure. On a mountain, water boils at a lower temperature.
quiz.3.q: The critical temperatures of some gases are given. Which one can be liquefied at 25 °C just by raising the pressure?
quiz.3.e: A substance liquefies under pressure only while it is below its critical temperature. 25 °C is below the critical temperature of NH₃ only. So at room temperature NH₃ is a vapor.
quiz.3.y.0: 25 °C is above CH₄'s critical temperature. CH₄ must first be cooled below −82 °C.
quiz.3.y.2: Helium's critical temperature is −268 °C. At 25 °C no pressure can liquefy it.
quiz.3.y.3: At 25 °C, H₂ is far above its critical temperature. Pressure alone is not enough.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Melt a solid, pour honey and boil water at different pressures.
A:adimlar.0.metin: In salt the particles form an ordered lattice. In glass they are arranged at random. We will heat both.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Which one melts all at once at a definite temperature?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Glass is an amorphous solid. It has no definite melting point and softens first.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Salt melts all at once at 801 °C, and its temperature stays constant until it has all melted. Glass softens slowly, with no definite melting point.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: One has an ordered lattice and the other does not. Could they melt the same way?
A:adimlar.1.metin: Heat the honey and fill the glass in 10 seconds.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: Heat the honey and play again.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: In warm honey the particles overcome attraction more easily and slide past each other quickly. So the viscosity drops.
A:adimlar.2.metin: In a closed container, molecules that escape from the liquid form a vapor. The pressure of this vapor is called vapor pressure. Change the temperature and the amount of liquid.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: At the same temperature, what happens to the vapor pressure if you add more water to the container?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Increase the amount of liquid and look at the gauge. Check whether the value changes.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: More liquid does not reduce the vapor. Try it with the counter.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Vapor pressure depends only on temperature and the type of liquid. The amount of liquid, the container's volume and the surface area do not change it. It rises quickly with temperature, though. For water it is 55 mmHg at 40 °C and 760 mmHg at 100 °C.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Heat the water in the pot and watch the temperature, the graph and the two pressures. You can also change the outside pressure. Find the following yourself.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.0.yazi: Heat the water at 1 atm until it boils. While it boils you keep heating. What does the temperature do?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.0.tamam: The water boiled at 100 °C, and the temperature stayed constant. The heat added no longer raises the temperature. It turns liquid into vapor. This temperature at 1 atm is called the normal boiling point.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.1.yazi: Lower the outside pressure to 0.5 atm, as if you were high on a mountain. At what temperature does the water boil?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.1.tamam: The water boiled at about 81 °C. Less heating was enough for the vapor pressure to reach the outside pressure. On Everest (about 0.3 atm) water boils at about 70 °C, and pasta cooks poorly.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.2.yazi: Raise the outside pressure to 2 atm, like a pressure cooker, and boil it again.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.2.tamam: The water boiled at about 121 °C, because the boiling point rises as outside pressure rises. Food cooks faster in hotter water.
A:adimlar.4.metin: When its state changes, a substance either absorbs heat or releases it. Go through the changes one by one.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: Why does sweat cool you as it evaporates?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: Evaporation takes heat from the skin
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Evaporation is endothermic, and it takes the heat it needs from the skin, so the skin cools down. When humidity is high, sweat evaporates poorly and you cannot cool off.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The changes that release heat are freezing, condensation and deposition. Find evaporation.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Sweat is at body temperature. The cooling comes from the change of state.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Dry ice (solid CO₂) does not melt at 1 atm. It turns straight into gas. Apply pressure to turn CO₂ at −20 °C into a liquid.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: At −20 °C, CO₂ liquefies above about 20 atm. Its triple point is at 5.1 atm, so liquid CO₂ cannot exist at 1 atm, and that is why dry ice sublimes. Above the critical temperature (31 °C), no pressure can liquefy it.
A:kapanis.0: Crystalline solids melt sharply at a definite temperature. Amorphous solids such as glass and plastic melt by softening.
A:kapanis.1: Viscosity is resistance to flow. With strong attraction between molecules, viscosity is high, and it drops when the liquid warms up.
A:kapanis.2: Vapor pressure rises with temperature and depends on the type of liquid. It does not depend on the amount of liquid.
A:kapanis.3: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the outside pressure. On a mountain water boils below 100 °C, and in a pressure cooker above it.
A:kapanis.4: Melting, evaporation and sublimation absorb heat. Freezing, condensation and deposition release heat.
